title: User Mode, Kernel Mode, System Calls and Interrupts
oneLiner: Why your code can't touch the disk directly, how it asks the kernel to, and how hardware gets the CPU's attention.
keyTakeaway: The CPU runs your code in user mode, where privileged instructions and other processes' memory are off limits. To read a file, send a packet or start a process, code makes a system call: a special instruction that switches the CPU into kernel mode at a fixed entry point the kernel controls. Interrupts are how devices and the timer get the CPU's attention, and exceptions such as page faults are how the CPU reports a problem with the current instruction. All three enter the kernel the same way: through a table of handlers the kernel set up at boot.
explanation:
Modern CPUs have at least two privilege levels. On x86 these are rings: the kernel runs in ring 0 (kernel mode), applications in ring 3 (user mode). ARM calls them exception levels, EL1 and EL0. In user mode the CPU refuses privileged instructions, such as disabling interrupts, changing page tables (the OS's map of which memory each process may use) or talking to I/O devices directly, and the page tables mark kernel memory as off limits. Try one anyway and the CPU raises an exception, the kernel takes over, and your process is usually killed. That hardware enforcement is what makes processes isolated from each other and from the kernel, rather than isolated by convention.

A system call is the controlled door between the two. Your C# File.ReadAllBytes eventually calls the C library's read wrapper, which puts a syscall number and arguments in registers (the CPU's own tiny storage slots) and executes the syscall instruction (svc on ARM64). The CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to the kernel's entry point, never to an address the caller chose. The kernel checks the arguments (is this file descriptor, the number the OS handed out for an open file, yours; is that buffer, the block of memory the data goes into, in your memory), does the work, puts a result or error code in a register, and returns to user mode. On Linux, open, read, write, mmap, fork, execve and exit are all system calls; on Windows, programs call documented Win32 APIs that wrap undocumented Nt* system calls.

A system call costs a mode switch, roughly a hundred nanoseconds to a microsecond with today's security mitigations, which is far more than a function call. That's why buffered I/O exists (one write of 64 KB instead of 65,536 writes of one byte) and why Linux maps some read-only calls such as clock_gettime into user space through the vDSO, so they need no mode switch at all. A mode switch isn't a context switch: the same thread keeps running, just with more privilege. A context switch only happens if the kernel decides to run a different thread, for example because the read has to wait for the disk.

Interrupts are asynchronous: a device raises one when something happens, such as a key press, a packet arriving or a disk read completing. The CPU finishes its current instruction, saves where it was, switches to kernel mode and runs that interrupt's handler from the interrupt descriptor table. The timer interrupt matters most to scheduling: it fires every few milliseconds, which is how the kernel takes the CPU back from a thread that never makes a system call. Exceptions are synchronous: the current instruction caused them. A page fault (touching memory that isn't currently mapped in), a divide by zero and a breakpoint are all exceptions, and on x86 the int3 breakpoint and the old int 0x80 system call path are called traps because they're deliberate.

Interview framing: user programs request privileged work through system calls, the hardware enforces the boundary, and the kernel is entered only through system calls, interrupts and exceptions. Virtual memory, which is what makes another process's memory unreachable, is covered in Virtual Memory, Paging and Cache Locality.
